situation: Djibrilla looks at a world map in his atlas. He notices that the west coast of Africa and the east coast of South America look like two pieces of a puzzle.
The Atlantic Ocean separates the two continents by thousands of kilometres. Djibrilla wonders if they were once joined together.
sitQA: What is the problem raised in the situation above?
The problem is that Djibrilla wonders if Africa and South America were once joined together.
Which ocean separates Africa and South America?
How can Djibrilla test his idea?
He can cut out the two continents from a map and fit them together, and read about the evidence found by scientists.
end.justification: This lesson will help us to understand that the continents were once joined and have moved slowly to their present positions.

qa.q: What is the theory of continental drift, and who proposed it?
qa.a: It is the theory that the continents were once joined in one great landmass and have slowly moved apart. It was proposed by Alfred Wegener, a German scientist, in 1912.

qa.q: What name did Wegener give to the single great landmass?
qa.a: He called it Pangaea, which means "all lands". It was surrounded by one great ocean called Panthalassa.
About 200 million years ago, it split into Laurasia in the north and Gondwanaland in the south. Later, these broke into the continents of today.

sum.title: I. The Theory of Continental Drift
defs: Continental drift is the theory that the continents were once joined in one landmass, Pangaea, and have slowly moved apart. It was proposed by Alfred Wegener in 1912.
items: Illustration: the Break-up of Pangaea
– About 200 million years ago, Pangaea began to break up.
– It split into Laurasia (north) and Gondwanaland (south).
– Africa, South America, India, Australia and Antarctica came from Gondwanaland.
– The continents are still moving a few centimetres each year.

qa.title: Question 1
qa.q: Look at the map. What does it show about Africa and South America?
qa.a: The coasts of Africa and South America fit together like the pieces of a jigsaw puzzle. This suggests that they were once joined.

qa.q: Fossils of Mesosaurus, a small freshwater reptile, are found in Brazil and in southern Africa. What does this prove?
qa.a: This small reptile could not swim across the ocean. So the two continents were joined when it lived.

qa.q: Scratches of ancient ice sheets are found in hot lands like southern Africa and India. What does this show?
qa.a: It shows that these lands were once joined together near the South Pole, where there was ice.

sum.title: II. Evidence for Continental Drift
sum.intro: Wegener gave four main types of evidence:
items: A. The Jigsaw Fit
The coasts of Africa and South America fit together like the pieces of a puzzle.
jigsaw_fit.png
B. Fossil Evidence
The same fossils, such as the reptile Mesosaurus and the plant Glossopteris, are found on continents now separated by oceans.
C. Rocks and Mountains
Rocks of the same type and age, and old mountain ranges, match on both sides of the Atlantic Ocean.
D. Glacial Evidence
Marks of ancient ice sheets are found in hot lands such as southern Africa, India and Australia.

evaluation: Pangaea was the single great landmass in which all the continents were joined.
Into which two landmasses did Pangaea split?
It split into Laurasia in the north and Gondwanaland in the south.
Give two pieces of evidence for continental drift.
The jigsaw fit of the coasts and the same fossils found on different continents.
remediation: The theory of continental drift was proposed by Alfred ______.
The single great landmass was called ______.
The fit of the coasts is called the ______ fit.
Pangaea began to break up about ______ million years ago.
end.homework: Listen to the news or ask an adult about a recent earthquake or volcanic eruption in the world. Write the name of the country and what happened.
end.homeworkTag: This prepares Lesson 10: The Theory of Plate Tectonics.
teacherNote: Checked: Wegener presented the theory in 1912 (book in 1915). Pangaea began to break up about 200 million years ago. The map uses the Bullard fit (1965) of the continental shelves.
Wegener could not explain what moves the continents. This is why his theory was rejected at first. Plate tectonics (next lesson) gives the explanation.
